title: Henry IV, Part 2
author: William Shakespeare
setting: England between the battle of Shrewsbury in 1403 and the coronation of Henry V in 1413: Warkworth, Eastcheap, Gaultree Forest, a Gloucestershire orchard and the Jerusalem Chamber at Westminster
lengthNote: Around 3,400 lines, more than half of them prose, with an Induction spoken by Rumour and an Epilogue
openingLine: Open your ears; for which of you will stop The vent of hearing when loud Rumour speaks?
summary: The sequel begins with a lie: Rumour tells Northumberland that his son won at Shrewsbury, and the truth arrives a scene later. Everything after that runs on delay and bad news. The king cannot sleep, Falstaff cannot pay, the rebels are tricked out of their army with a promise, and two old justices in Gloucestershire count their dead friends and the price of bullocks at Stamford fair. Hal takes the crown from his father's pillow before the man is dead, and in the last scene the new king walks past the old friend who has ridden all night to meet him. It is the play where Part 1's jokes come back with the cost attached.

sourceText.label: Globe/Moby text of Henry IV, Part 2
sourceText.note: Line numbers follow the traditional Globe numbering, which counts prose lines as printed. Rumour's Induction is numbered separately from Act I. Modern editions vary.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: Soon after Part 1, and before Henry V, which the Epilogue promises.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: One quarto, surviving in two states: the second adds a scene the first omits, the king's sleepless night in 3.1.

atAGlance.label: The Folio
atAGlance.note: Adds passages the quarto lacks, including Lady Percy's speech about Hotspur and much of the Archbishop's case, and cuts some of the oaths.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.value: Induction, five acts and an Epilogue
atAGlance.note: The Epilogue promises more of Falstaff and admits, in passing, that the knight was once called Oldcastle.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: False news, a sick earl and a knight in debt
structure.summary: Rumour, painted full of tongues, tells the audience what it is about to do and then does it: Northumberland hears that Hotspur is alive and victorious, then that he is dead. Falstaff, walking London with a page and a diagnosis, meets the Lord Chief Justice, who wanted him for the Gadshill robbery and cannot now touch him because of the war. At York the Archbishop turns a sermon into a rebellion.

scenes.title: Rumour
scenes.summary: A figure covered in painted tongues explains that the wrong news of Shrewsbury is on its way to Warkworth.

scenes.title: Warkworth
scenes.summary: Three reports reach Northumberland in succession; the last, from Morton, is true, and the earl calls for order to die.

scenes.title: A London street
scenes.summary: Falstaff asks his page what the doctor said about his water, and then out-talks the Lord Chief Justice.

scenes.title: The Archbishop's palace
scenes.summary: The rebels count the king's three armies and decide to fight anyway, without waiting for Northumberland.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: The Boar's Head grows old
structure.summary: The Hostess has Falstaff arrested for debt and is talked out of it inside a hundred lines. Hal, back in London, is ashamed of wanting small beer and of being unable to mourn a father in front of Poins. At Warkworth Lady Percy stops her father-in-law going to war by describing the son he failed to help. The tavern scene that follows has Doll Tearsheet, Pistol drawing on a whore, and a prince who listens to himself being described as a shallow young fellow.

scenes.title: The arrest
scenes.summary: Fang and Snare try to take Falstaff; Mistress Quickly recites the day he promised to marry her, and lends him more money.

scenes.title: Hal and Poins
scenes.summary: The prince confesses that keeping vile company has taken away his right to grieve, and agrees to spy on Falstaff as a drawer.

scenes.title: Warkworth again
scenes.summary: Lady Percy's account of Hotspur, the glass in which the noble youth dressed themselves, persuades Northumberland to run to Scotland.

scenes.title: The Boar's Head
scenes.summary: Doll asks when Falstaff will patch up his old body for heaven; Pistol is thrown downstairs; Hal is called to the wars.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: A king awake, and two justices remembering
structure.summary: Henry IV walks his palace at night and envies the ship-boy asleep on the mast. Warwick reminds him that Richard II foresaw all of this. The scene was missing from the first printing. It is followed by the Gloucestershire orchard, where Shallow and Silence ask after old acquaintances who are dead, price livestock, and let Falstaff choose his recruits by whether they can pay to be excused.

scenes.title: Sleep
scenes.summary: The king asks why sleep visits the wet sea-boy and not him, and hears that the rebels are said to be fifty thousand strong.

scenes.title: Shallow's house
scenes.summary: Mouldy, Shadow, Wart, Feeble and Bullcalf are pricked; the two who bribe Bardolph go home; the chimes at midnight are remembered.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: Gaultree Forest and the Jerusalem Chamber
structure.summary: Prince John promises that every grievance will be redressed, waits until the rebel army has dispersed on the strength of the promise, and arrests its leaders for treason. Falstaff captures a knight who surrenders to his reputation and praises sherris sack. At Westminster the news of victory makes the king worse, not better. Hal, thinking him dead, carries the crown into the next room; the king wakes and reads the act as the son wishing him gone.

scenes.title: The parley
scenes.summary: Westmoreland asks the Archbishop why he has turned his books to graves; the rebels hand over their articles.

scenes.title: The promise
scenes.summary: Prince John swears by the honour of his blood, the armies are discharged, and the rebel lords are arrested.

scenes.title: Sir John Colevile
scenes.summary: Falstaff takes a prisoner without fighting and, alone, explains why Prince John does not laugh.

scenes.title: The king's fit
scenes.summary: Good news from the north reaches a man too ill to receive it; he is carried into the Jerusalem Chamber.

scenes.title: The crown
scenes.summary: Hal takes the crown from the pillow, is accused of wishing his father dead, answers, and hears how the crown was got.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: The new king
structure.summary: Shallow shows Falstaff his household and Falstaff plans to keep the prince laughing with it for a year. The Lord Chief Justice waits to be dismissed and is instead confirmed and called a father. Falstaff hears of the accession in Shallow's orchard, borrows a thousand pounds, rides through the night and shouts to the coronation procession. The king tells him he does not know him. The Chief Justice takes him to the Fleet, and Prince John foresees a war in France.

scenes.title: Shallow's household
scenes.summary: Davy asks his master to countenance a knave; Falstaff studies how a man takes on the character of his servants.

scenes.title: The palace
scenes.summary: The new king tells the Chief Justice who once imprisoned him that he shall be as a father to his youth.

scenes.title: The orchard
scenes.summary: Pistol brings the news of Henry IV's death; Falstaff announces that the laws of England are at his commandment.

scenes.title: The beadles
scenes.summary: Doll and the Hostess are dragged off to prison, allegedly over a man beaten to death.

scenes.title: Near Westminster Abbey
scenes.summary: The king rejects Falstaff in public; the knight tells Shallow it was only a show, and is arrested.

characters.name: King Henry IV
characters.summary: He never leaves the palace in this play and never sleeps in it. Everything he says is retrospective: how he got the crown, what Richard prophesied, what the earl of Northumberland once was to him. His last speech to his son is a piece of advice on foreign policy, and his death fulfils a prophecy in the cheapest possible way, by the name of a room.
characters.clue: He envies a ship-boy asleep in the rigging, and he dies in a chamber named after a city he never reached.

characters.name: Prince Hal, later King Henry V
characters.summary: He is on stage far less than in Part 1, and every appearance is an argument about what he is allowed to feel. He cannot mourn his father in front of Poins because it would look like acting; he takes the crown too early and has to explain that it was grief. When he becomes king the first thing he does is adopt the judge who jailed him, and the second is to refuse to know Falstaff.
characters.clue: He is ashamed of wanting small beer, he tries on a crown from a pillow, and he tells an old man to fall to his prayers.

relationships.label: companion, then rejecter of
relationships.note: They share one tavern scene and one street, and he is silent for most of both.

characters.name: Sir John Falstaff
characters.role: A knight, in debt, with a page and a captain's commission
characters.summary: He enters asking about his urine and spends the play being told he is old, by the Chief Justice, by Doll, by his own mirror. He still wins every argument, but the arguments are now with women he owes money to and justices whose youth he can see the bottom of. His plan for the new reign is entirely serious, and its failure is the end of the play.
characters.clue: He tells a judge that he was born with a white head and a round belly, and rides all night to be told that a king does not know him.
traits: still the best talker in England

characters.name: The Lord Chief Justice
characters.role: Head of the king's bench, who once committed the prince
characters.summary: He is Falstaff's true opposite in this play, as Hotspur was in the last: an old man whose age is authority rather than decay. In 5.2 he expects to lose his office for having jailed the prince and argues his case as if to a jury, and the new king agrees with every word. The play makes law survive the change of reign by making a person survive it.
characters.clue: He once sent the heir to the throne to prison, and is told by the new king that the act was exactly right.

characters.name: Prince John of Lancaster
characters.role: The king's younger son, commanding at Gaultree
characters.summary: He swears by the honour of his blood that the rebels' grievances will be redressed, lets them send their army home, and then arrests them, explaining that he promised redress of grievances and not their lives. The play does not comment. Falstaff's verdict, that the boy does not drink and therefore cannot laugh, is the only judgement passed on him.
characters.clue: He keeps his promise to the letter and hangs the men he made it to.

characters.name: The Archbishop of York
characters.role: Richard Scroop, leader of the second rebellion
characters.summary: He is a rebel who makes his case as a physician: the commonwealth is sick of its own choice and must bleed. He also despises the people he needs, and says so, which is why his rising has no popular life in it. At Gaultree he hands over his articles like a man submitting a petition, and is executed as a traitor for it.
characters.clue: He turns his books to graves and his ink to blood, and accepts a prince's word for his redress.

characters.name: The Earl of Northumberland
characters.role: Hotspur's father, who was sick for Shrewsbury
characters.summary: He receives the news of his son's death in stages and answers it with a speech asking the world to end. Then his daughter-in-law reminds him that he was not there, and he goes to Scotland instead of to the Archbishop. The play gives him the largest grief and the smallest action.
characters.clue: He calls for order to die and then takes his crutch to Scotland.

characters.name: Lady Percy
characters.summary: She has one speech, and it is the play's memorial to Part 1: her husband as the mirror in which young men dressed, whose very speech defect was imitated. Its purpose is not tribute but accusation, aimed at the father who let him die, and it works.
characters.clue: She describes a dead man's limp and stammer being copied by the fashionable, and uses the picture to keep his father at home.

characters.name: Justice Shallow
characters.role: A Gloucestershire justice of the peace, Falstaff's old acquaintance
characters.summary: He remembers a youth he did not have, and Falstaff, who was there, says so to the audience. His scenes are the play's picture of ordinary time passing: the price of a yoke of bullocks, the dead at Clement's Inn, a servant asking that a knave be countenanced. He lends a thousand pounds on the strength of a friendship that ends in the next scene.
characters.clue: He asks whether an old acquaintance is dead, is told the price of ewes in the same breath, and lends a knight a thousand pounds.

relationships.label: lends to and is used by

characters.name: Doll Tearsheet
characters.role: A prostitute at the Boar's Head, with Mistress Quickly its hostess
characters.summary: She and the Hostess are the tavern in this play, since the prince has almost left it. Doll is the one person who tells Falstaff to his face that he is dying, and she does it with affection. In 5.4 she is dragged to prison by beadles while the coronation is being prepared, which is the play's comment on what the new order does with the old one.
characters.clue: She tells a fat knight to patch up his old body for heaven, and is hauled off by beadles on coronation day.

themes.name: Rumour and report
themes.summary: The play opens with a personification of false news and never afterwards lets anyone hear the truth first. Northumberland gets three reports of Shrewsbury; the rebels are told the king's forces are divided; the king is told of victory when he is past hearing it; Falstaff hears of the accession from Pistol, who cannot say it plainly. Knowledge arrives late, second-hand and wrong, and people act on it before it is corrected.
themes.development: Rumour announces the method in the Induction, the Archbishop calls the commonwealth sick of what it once believed in 1.3, and in 5.5 Falstaff acts on his own report of what the king will do.

themes.name: Age, sickness and time
themes.summary: Everyone in this play is older than the same person was in Part 1, and most of them are ill. The king's body is consumed by the crown, Northumberland is crafty-sick, Falstaff's doctor has an opinion on his water, and the Gloucestershire justices count their dead. The Chief Justice's inventory of an old man in 1.2 is the play's measure, and Falstaff fails every item on it except the voice.
themes.development: Falstaff turns diseases to commodity in 1.2; the king cannot buy sleep in 3.1; the chimes at midnight are recalled in 3.2; the young king in 5.5 calls white hairs on a jester ill-becoming.

themes.name: Fathers and sons
themes.summary: Northumberland loses a son he did not help; the king loses a son he cannot read; Falstaff is discarded by the prince who played his son at the Boar's Head; the Chief Justice is adopted in the same scene. The play settles the question Part 1 left open, which of Hal's fathers he will keep, and the answer is the one who sent him to prison.
themes.development: Lady Percy convicts Northumberland in 2.3, the king accuses Hal over the crown in 4.5, and in 5.2 the new king chooses a father in public.

themes.name: Legitimacy and the crooked ways to a crown
themes.summary: The dying king admits to his son, in private, what the rebels have been saying in public: that he met the crown by by-paths and indirect ways. The remedy he proposes is not repentance but a foreign war to occupy the minds that might remember. Hal inherits both the crown and the advice, and Prince John's last speech shows the advice being taken.
themes.development: The Archbishop recites the nation's second thoughts in 1.3, the king lists his own methods in 4.5, and the play's last lines look towards France.

themes.name: Law and the Chief Justice
themes.summary: Where Part 1 tested honour, this play tests the law. It is sworn by and broken at Gaultree, evaded in 1.2 because of the war, imagined abolished in 5.3 when Falstaff hears the news, and finally embodied in an old judge whom the new king chooses to keep. The rejection of Falstaff and the confirmation of the Chief Justice are the same act seen from two sides.
themes.development: The Chief Justice cannot touch Falstaff in 1.2; Prince John keeps the letter of his word in 4.2; the king adopts the judge in 5.2 and lets him commit Falstaff in 5.5.

themes.name: A country in parts
themes.summary: Part 2 adds a county to Part 1's map. Beside Westminster, Eastcheap and the rebel camp there is now Gloucestershire, where the war is a matter of which recruits can pay to stay home and the great events reach an orchard by way of a swaggerer with a headache. The play's England is a set of places that hear about each other late and do not understand what they hear.
themes.development: Warkworth, York and London each receive their own news in Act I; the orchard in 3.2 and 5.3 measures the reign in bullocks; the coronation in 5.5 brings all the parts to one street and sorts them.

themes.name: Performance and the public self
themes.summary: Hal's problem in this play is that any feeling he shows will be read as acting, since he has been acting since 1.2 of Part 1. The rejection scene is the same problem from the other side: the new king must be seen to change, so the change has to happen in a street, in front of a procession, to a man who has ridden all night. Falstaff's last defence is that it was a show, and for once he is wrong.
themes.development: Hal explains why he cannot mourn in 2.2, plays a drawer in 2.4, and in 5.5 performs the end of his youth so publicly that Falstaff mistakes it for theatre.

techniques.name: Direct address: Rumour and the Epilogue
techniques.definition: A speaker turning outward to address the audience by name.
techniques.inThisBook: The play is framed by two figures who talk to the theatre rather than the court: Rumour, who tells the audience its household is sitting in front of him, and an Epilogue that promises a sequel and apologises for a name.

techniques.name: Prose against verse
techniques.definition: Using the shift between metrical speech and prose to mark who is speaking and where.
techniques.inThisBook: The proportion has tilted since Part 1: prose now carries the tavern, the street, the orchard and Falstaff alone, and verse is left to the sick, the rebellious and the dying. The rejection is spoken in verse to a man who has only ever answered in prose.

techniques.name: Soliloquy
techniques.definition: A character alone on stage, speaking directly to the audience.
techniques.inThisBook: Two of the play's best speeches are its two soliloquies on the body: the king's on sleep in 3.1 and Falstaff's on sherris sack in 4.3, one a man who cannot rest and one a man explaining why he cannot be sober.

techniques.name: Disease and rot
techniques.definition: A body's sickness used as the play's image for the state of things.
techniques.inThisBook: The Archbishop says the commonwealth must bleed, the king's physicians are named, Falstaff's water is analysed in his first line, and the crown is called a golden care that keeps the ports of slumber open. Illness is not a metaphor here so much as the general condition.

techniques.name: Foil structure
techniques.definition: Building characters as deliberate answers to one another.
techniques.inThisBook: Part 1 set Falstaff against Hotspur; this play sets him against the Lord Chief Justice, another old man, and lets the prince choose. Shallow is a further foil, an old man who invents the wild youth Falstaff actually had.

techniques.name: The crown on the pillow
techniques.definition: An object handled on stage that carries more than its use in the scene explains.
techniques.inThisBook: The crown is lifted from a sleeping man's pillow, carried into the next room, missed, recovered and argued over, and the argument is the whole relationship of father and son. Henry IV calls it polished perturbation and a bedfellow; Hal answers that he tried it on as an enemy.

quotations.text: Open your ears; for which of you will stop The vent of hearing when loud Rumour speaks?
quotations.speaker: Rumour
quotations.context: The first words of the play, spoken by a figure painted full of tongues.
quotations.analysis: The command and the question cancel each other: nobody can stop their ears, so the order is unnecessary, and Rumour knows it. The play begins by making the audience complicit in the thing it is about to watch go wrong, and 'vent' turns the ear into a vent-hole in a cask, something news simply pours through.

quotations.text: Rumour is a pipe Blown by surmises, jealousies, conjectures And of so easy and so plain a stop That the blunt monster with uncounted heads, The still-discordant wavering multitude, Can play upon it.
quotations.speaker: Rumour
quotations.context: Rumour describes himself before revealing that he is on his way to Warkworth.
quotations.analysis: The musical image is precise: a pipe with an easy stop is one any child can finger. Three abstract nouns blow it, and then the player turns out to be the crowd, described as a monster in the same breath that the Archbishop will use two scenes later. The play's contempt for the multitude is shared by its rebels and its personifications alike.

quotations.text: Let heaven kiss earth! now let not Nature's hand Keep the wild flood confined! let order die!
quotations.speaker: Northumberland
quotations.context: On finally learning that Hotspur is dead and the rebellion broken.
quotations.analysis: A father's grief is expressed as a political programme, which is the play's way of showing how little separates the two in this family. The imperatives are addressed to nobody who can carry them out, and the earl's actual response, a scene later, is to go to Scotland. The gap between the speech and the deed is the whole of his character.

quotations.text: I am not only witty in myself, but the cause that wit is in other men.
quotations.speaker: Falstaff
quotations.context: To his page, on the fact that his own size provokes jokes wherever he goes.
quotations.analysis: It is a claim to be a natural resource rather than a person, and the play spends five acts proving it true: Hal, Poins, Doll, the Chief Justice and Shallow are all at their best when talking about him. The sentence is also his defence against ageing, since a cause does not need to be young.

quotations.text: you are as a candle, the better part burnt out.
quotations.speaker: The Lord Chief Justice
quotations.context: In the middle of the Chief Justice's inventory of Falstaff's age.
quotations.analysis: The judge's list of what an old man has, a moist eye, a dry hand, a yellow cheek, a white beard, is the play's first medical examination, and this is its summary. Falstaff's reply, that he is a wassail candle and all tallow, accepts the image and changes what it is for: a tallow candle is not made to last but to light a feast.

quotations.text: it was alway yet the trick of our English nation, if they have a good thing, to make it too common.
quotations.speaker: Falstaff
quotations.context: Complaining to the Chief Justice that he has been sent to the wars again.
quotations.analysis: He is describing himself as a national asset in danger of overuse, and the line is also a fair description of what happened to Falstaff between the two parts, a popular character brought back for more. The complaint that he cannot last for ever, a few words earlier, is the nearest he comes in the whole play to admitting what Doll and the Chief Justice tell him.

quotations.text: I will turn diseases to commodity.
quotations.speaker: Falstaff
quotations.context: Alone, at the end of the scene, having decided to use his gout as an excuse for limping and his limp as evidence of war service.
quotations.analysis: Commodity is a trading word, and the sentence is a business plan: an ailment will be marketed as a wound. It is the play's economy in miniature. Everything in it, sleep, honour, a promise at Gaultree, a thousand pounds, is being converted into something else, and Falstaff is merely the most candid trader.

quotations.text: The commonwealth is sick of their own choice; Their over-greedy love hath surfeited: An habitation giddy and unsure Hath he that buildeth on the vulgar heart.
quotations.speaker: The Archbishop of York
quotations.context: Justifying the rebellion to the other lords, before deciding to march without Northumberland.
quotations.analysis: The rebel's grievance is not that Bolingbroke was chosen wrongly but that the people who chose him have changed their minds, and the speech goes on to abuse them for it. The diagnosis of surfeit repeats the king's own language about Richard, so both sides in this war describe the country as a patient who has eaten too much of what it wanted.

quotations.text: Doth it not show vilely in me to desire small beer?
quotations.speaker: Prince Hal
quotations.context: His first line in the play, to Poins, on being tired.
quotations.analysis: The prince's re-entry is a question about whether a taste for weak beer is a fault of character, and it announces the play's version of him: a man watching himself from outside. The word 'vilely' is doing the work, since it makes a small preference a moral matter, and the rest of the scene follows the same line into whether he is allowed to grieve.

quotations.text: let the end try the man.
quotations.speaker: Prince Hal
quotations.context: To Poins, who has said the prince would be a hypocrite to mourn a father he has never obeyed.
quotations.analysis: Six words that ask to be judged later, which is the request Hal has been making since the sun soliloquy in Part 1. 'Try' is a legal and metallurgical word at once, a case heard and a metal tested, and the play grants the request in 5.5 in a form neither Poins nor the audience is comfortable with.

quotations.text: Did all the chivalry of England move To do brave acts: he was indeed the glass Wherein the noble youth did dress themselves:
quotations.speaker: Lady Percy
quotations.context: Reminding Northumberland what his son was, and that he was left to die.
quotations.analysis: The speech is the play's memorial to Hotspur, and it is a memorial to fashion rather than to war: young men copied his walk and his thick speech. A mirror is where you dress, not where you fight. The Folio adds the passage; the quarto does not have it, so the two early texts differ over how much the play looks back.

quotations.text: Peace, good Doll! do not speak like a death's-head; do not bid me remember mine end.
quotations.speaker: Falstaff
quotations.context: Doll has just asked when he will stop fighting by day and foining by night and patch up his old body for heaven.
quotations.analysis: A death's-head was a skull carved on a ring, worn as a reminder of mortality, so he is asking a prostitute not to be jewellery. The request is tender and it is refused by the whole scene, in which the prince overhears himself abused and the drums call Falstaff to a war he will not fight in.

quotations.text: How many thousand of my poorest subjects Are at this hour asleep! O sleep, O gentle sleep, Nature's soft nurse, how have I frighted thee, That thou no more wilt weigh my eyelids down And steep my senses in forgetfulness?
quotations.speaker: King Henry IV
quotations.context: Alone in his nightgown at Westminster, having sent for Warwick and Surrey.
quotations.analysis: The king begins by counting his subjects and ends by envying them, and the thing he envies is forgetfulness, which for a man with his history is not a small thing. The scene was absent from the first state of the 1600 quarto, so the play's most famous speech was for a time not in the play at all.

quotations.text: Uneasy lies the head that wears a crown.
quotations.speaker: King Henry IV
quotations.context: The last line of the soliloquy on sleep.
quotations.analysis: The line has become a proverb, which hides how odd it is in place: it follows twenty lines about a ship-boy asleep in a storm, so the crown is being compared to a mast. 'Lies' quietly carries its other meaning too, since this king's head has been lying since Richard II, and the play's next scene is about a justice who lies about his youth.

quotations.text: We have heard the chimes at midnight, Master Shallow.
quotations.speaker: Falstaff
quotations.context: Shallow has been recalling the mad days of their youth at Clement's Inn.
quotations.analysis: Shallow asks whether they have seen the days, and Falstaff answers with what they heard, which is a sound of lateness. The sentence is nostalgic and corrective at once, and a few lines later, alone, Falstaff tells the audience the justice is lying about all of it. Orson Welles took the line for the title of his film because it is where the two Henry IV plays turn to look back.

quotations.text: By my troth, I care not; a man can die but once: we owe God a death: I'll ne'er bear a base mind:
quotations.speaker: Feeble
quotations.context: The woman's tailor, pressed for the war, refuses to bribe his way out as Mouldy and Bullcalf have done.
quotations.analysis: The commonplace that Hal used on Falstaff before Shrewsbury is here given to the weakest recruit on the stage, and he means it. Feeble is the play's answer to the catechism on honour: a man with nothing to gain who accepts the debt, in prose, in an orchard. His name is the joke and his line is not.

quotations.text: Lord, Lord, how subject we old men are to this vice of lying!
quotations.speaker: Falstaff
quotations.context: Alone after the recruiting, having watched Shallow reminisce.
quotations.analysis: The first-person plural is the giveaway: he includes himself, and the audience has been counting his lies since Gadshill. But the lies he means are Shallow's inventions of a youth he never had, and the speech goes on to describe what the justice actually looked like at Clement's Inn, which is the play's one piece of straight memory.

quotations.text: Turning your books to graves, your ink to blood, Your pens to lances and your tongue divine To a trumpet and a point of war?
quotations.speaker: Westmoreland
quotations.context: Asking the Archbishop, at the parley in Gaultree Forest, why a churchman has taken up arms.
quotations.analysis: Four conversions in three lines, each turning a thing of the study into a thing of the field, and the question is not really answered. The Archbishop replies that everyone is diseased, which is a different subject. The passage is one of those the 1600 quarto omits, so the rebels' case for themselves is fuller in the Folio.

quotations.text: we are all diseased, And with our surfeiting and wanton hours Have brought ourselves into a burning fever, And we must bleed for it;
quotations.speaker: The Archbishop of York
quotations.context: Answering Westmoreland at the parley.
quotations.analysis: Bleeding was the standard treatment for a fever, so the rebellion is presented as medicine rather than war, and the patient is everybody. The metaphor is the same one the king uses in his own bedchamber and Falstaff uses about his water, which means the play's three most different men agree on its diagnosis and differ only about the cure.

quotations.text: My lord, these griefs shall be with speed redress'd; Upon my soul, they shall. If this may please you, Discharge your powers unto their several counties, As we will ours:
quotations.speaker: Prince John of Lancaster
quotations.context: Accepting the rebels' articles at Gaultree.
quotations.analysis: Every word is kept. The griefs are redressed, and the men who brought them are arrested for treason a hundred lines later, on the ground that a promise about grievances is not a promise about persons. The oath on his soul is the part that sticks, and Shakespeare gives no one on stage a line of protest, so the audience has to supply it.

quotations.text: A good sherris sack hath a two-fold operation in it.
quotations.speaker: Falstaff
quotations.context: Alone, having decided that Prince John does not love him because the boy drinks no wine.
quotations.analysis: The speech that follows is a mock-medical lecture, with the wine ascending to the brain and warming the liver, and it is the last time Falstaff holds the stage alone at length. Its conclusion, that if he had a thousand sons he would teach them to forswear thin drink, is a father's advice, delivered by a man about to lose the only son he has.

quotations.text: O polish'd perturbation! golden care! That keep'st the ports of slumber open wide To many a watchful night!
quotations.speaker: Prince Hal
quotations.context: Alone with his sleeping father, looking at the crown on the pillow.
quotations.analysis: He addresses the crown as his father addressed sleep, and the two speeches answer each other across an act: the one thing keeps the other away. The pairing of a Latinate abstraction with a plain adjective, 'polish'd perturbation', is a habit the son shares with the father, and it is the closest they come to a conversation before the king wakes and misreads him.

quotations.text: Thou hast stolen that which after some few hours Were thine without offence; and at my death Thou hast seal'd up my expectation:
quotations.speaker: King Henry IV
quotations.context: The king, awake, finds the crown gone and his son returned with it.
quotations.analysis: The accusation is theft, and it comes from the one man in England who knows what stealing a crown feels like. 'Seal'd up' is the language of a will, so the son's act is read as a signature on a document the father never wanted to sign. The scene turns only when Hal, in reply, admits that he spoke to the crown as to an enemy.

quotations.text: God knows, my son, By what by-paths and indirect crook'd ways I met this crown; and I myself know well How troublesome it sat upon my head.
quotations.speaker: King Henry IV
quotations.context: The dying king's last counsel to his heir.
quotations.analysis: 'Met' is the word to notice. He does not say took or won: the crown is something he encountered on a road, as if the deposition of Richard had been an accident of travel. The confession is private, made to one person, and the political advice that follows it is designed to make sure nobody else asks the question.

quotations.text: Therefore, my Harry, Be it thy course to busy giddy minds With foreign quarrels; that action, hence borne out, May waste the memory of the former days.
quotations.speaker: King Henry IV
quotations.context: The practical conclusion of the deathbed speech.
quotations.analysis: This is the sentence Henry V is built on. A foreign war is prescribed as a way of wearing out memory, so the campaign in France begins here as a treatment for the usurpation rather than as a claim. Prince John's last speech in the play, foreseeing the civil swords carried abroad, shows the prescription being filled.

quotations.text: It hath been prophesied to me many years, I should not die but in Jerusalem; Which vainly I supposed the Holy Land: But bear me to that chamber; there I'll lie; In that Jerusalem shall Harry die.
quotations.speaker: King Henry IV
quotations.context: On learning that the room he fell ill in is called the Jerusalem Chamber.
quotations.analysis: The crusade that opened Part 1 ends in a name on a door. The prophecy is fulfilled exactly and worthlessly, in the manner of the apparitions in Macbeth, and the king seems almost relieved by the joke. 'Vainly' means both mistakenly and in vain, and the line allows him both meanings at once.

quotations.text: This new and gorgeous garment, majesty, Sits not so easy on me as you think.
quotations.speaker: King Henry V
quotations.context: His first words as king, to his brothers, who are afraid of him.
quotations.analysis: Kingship is a suit of clothes, and the tailor's word 'sits' does the work. The image completes a sequence that began with the crown as a bedfellow and continued with the crown tried on as an enemy: the son takes up his father's habit of treating majesty as an object that presses on the body, but he wears it rather than lies beside it.

quotations.text: You shall be as a father to my youth: My voice shall sound as you do prompt mine ear, And I will stoop and humble my intents To your well-practised wise directions.
quotations.speaker: King Henry V
quotations.context: To the Lord Chief Justice, who expected to be dismissed for having imprisoned the prince.
quotations.analysis: The adoption is public and it is the answer to the question both parts have been asking. 'Prompt' is a theatre word: the judge will feed the king his lines from the wings. The old man who is chosen and the old man who is rejected three scenes later are the same shape on stage, white-haired, once feared, and the king's two speeches to them are built to be compared.

quotations.text: The tide of blood in me Hath proudly flow'd in vanity till now: Now doth it turn and ebb back to the sea, Where it shall mingle with the state of floods
quotations.speaker: King Henry V
quotations.context: Announcing his reformation to the court and the Chief Justice.
quotations.analysis: The reformation is described as a tide, which is to say as something that happens by itself and on schedule, and the speech was designed in Part 1. Water imagery has followed the family: the father asked for the wild flood to be confined, and Northumberland asked for it to be released; the son presents himself as its natural return to the sea.

quotations.text: the laws of England are at my commandment. Blessed are they that have been my friends; and woe to my lord chief-justice!
quotations.speaker: Falstaff
quotations.context: In Shallow's orchard, on hearing that Hal is king, calling for any man's horses.
quotations.analysis: It is the exact fear that the Chief Justice voiced in the palace one scene earlier, spoken aloud by the man he feared, and the play has arranged the two scenes so the audience hears the answer before the question. The beatitude, 'Blessed are they', turns Falstaff's coming reign into a parody sermon, which is how Hal will describe the man in the next scene.

quotations.text: I know thee not, old man: fall to thy prayers; How ill white hairs become a fool and jester!
quotations.speaker: King Henry V
quotations.context: In the street outside the Abbey, after Falstaff has called out to him from the crowd.
quotations.analysis: The first sentence is a lie and the second is a diagnosis, and the play has spent five acts making the diagnosis true: everybody has been telling Falstaff about his white hairs. The king speaks in verse to a man who has only ever answered in prose, and the metre is the wall between them. The Globe text prints the speaker as Henry IV, a slip that the two parts almost invite.

quotations.text: Presume not that I am the thing I was; For God doth know, so shall the world perceive, That I have turn'd away my former self; So will I those that kept me company.
quotations.speaker: King Henry V
quotations.context: The continuation of the rejection.
quotations.analysis: He turns away a self as if it were a person, and then turns away the persons. The phrase 'so shall the world perceive' says why the scene has to happen in a street: the reformation is worthless unless witnessed. It is the sun soliloquy of Part 1 carried out in public, with the base contagious clouds standing four yards away.

quotations.text: Master Shallow, I owe you a thousand pound.
quotations.speaker: Falstaff
quotations.context: His first words after the king has passed on.
quotations.analysis: He does not answer the king; he answers his creditor, and the first thing the rejection produces is an admission of debt. The play has run on credit since Mistress Quickly's arrest in 2.1, and here the account is finally acknowledged by a man who has never once paid. Shallow's reply is to ask for it back, which is what everyone in this play wants and nobody gets.

timeline.label: The battle of Shrewsbury
timeline.detail: Fought on 21 July; the play opens with the news of it reaching Warkworth wrongly and then rightly.

timeline.label: Archbishop Scrope's rising ends at Shipton Moor
timeline.detail: The rebels disbanded on a promise of redress and their leaders were executed; the play sets the meeting in Gaultree Forest.

timeline.label: Northumberland killed at Bramham Moor
timeline.detail: The earl who fled to Scotland in 2.3 was killed in a last rising; the play reports his defeat in a single message in 4.4.

timeline.label: Henry IV dies at Westminster; Henry V is crowned
timeline.detail: The king died on 20 March in the abbot's lodging, in the room called the Jerusalem Chamber, and his son was crowned on 9 April.

timeline.label: Hall's Union of the Two Noble Families
timeline.detail: The chronicle that gave the Tudor histories their shape, and the Gaultree trick its account.

timeline.label: Holinshed's Chronicles reissued
timeline.detail: The second edition is Shakespeare's principal source for the rising of 1405 and the king's last illness.

timeline.label: Part 1 printed, and Part 2 probably on stage
timeline.detail: The second part is usually dated to about 1597-98, following the success of the first; the Epilogue's promise of Henry V looks forward to 1599.

timeline.label: The quarto
timeline.detail: Entered in the Stationers' Register in August and printed the same year in two states, the second of them adding the king's sleepless scene in 3.1.

timeline.label: The First Folio
timeline.detail: Adds several passages the quarto lacks and removes many of its oaths; the two texts give editors a play of two slightly different sizes.

timeline.label: Orson Welles films Chimes at Midnight
timeline.detail: Shot in Spain and built from both parts of Henry IV around Welles's own Falstaff, with the rejection as its destination.

timeline.label: The Hollow Crown on television
timeline.detail: Richard Eyre's films of both parts, with Jeremy Irons as the king, Tom Hiddleston as Hal and Simon Russell Beale as Falstaff.

places.name: Warkworth Castle, Northumberland
places.note: Where the false and then the true news of Shrewsbury reaches the earl, and where his daughter-in-law persuades him not to fight.

places.name: Eastcheap, London
places.note: The Boar's Head, now the scene of an arrest for debt, a fight with Pistol and Doll on Falstaff's knee.

places.name: York
places.note: The Archbishop's palace, where the second rebellion is argued into existence.

places.name: Galtres Forest, north of York
places.note: The play's Gaultree, where Prince John's promise disbands an army.

places.name: Westminster Abbey, London
places.note: The Jerusalem Chamber, in the abbot's lodging, where Henry IV died and where the play has him fulfil his prophecy.

places.name: Gloucestershire
places.note: Justice Shallow's house and orchard, where recruits are pricked and the accession is announced; the play names the county but no village.

criticalViews.position: The rejection as necessary and right
criticalViews.summary: A long tradition reads the last scene as the completion of the education begun in Part 1: the prince must be seen to leave misrule behind, the Chief Justice is the state's continuity, and Falstaff has told us himself what he intends to do with the laws of England.
criticalViews.counter: The play gives the rejection to a street rather than a council chamber and follows it with beadles and the Fleet, which is more punishment than the argument needs.

criticalViews.position: A play about ageing rather than politics
criticalViews.summary: Criticism attentive to the Gloucestershire scenes and the sickbed reads the play as an elegy: the subject is time, the tone is autumnal, and the political plot is a frame around Shallow's dead friends and Falstaff's white hairs.
criticalViews.counter: Gaultree Forest is not elegiac at all, and the play's cold centre, Prince John's kept promise, has nothing to do with age.

criticalViews.summary: Editors have long argued about whether Part 2 was planned from the start or written to profit from Part 1's success, and the play's habit of repeating its predecessor's shapes, a tavern scene, a recruiting scene, a father's interview, is evidence for both sides.
criticalViews.counter: Whatever was planned, the repetitions are darker each time, which argues for design rather than accident.

essayQuestions.question: Is the rejection of Falstaff a betrayal or a necessity?
essayQuestions.focus: The last scene and everything that leads to it
plan: Begin with what Falstaff says he will do with power in 5.3, and what the Chief Justice fears in 5.2, so the scene's political necessity is on the table.
Set that against 2.4, where Doll and the Hostess give the tavern a life the state has no use for, and 5.4, where the beadles arrive.
Examine the language of 5.5: verse to a prose speaker, 'I know thee not', and the promise of an allowance.
Consider Prince John's kept promise at Gaultree as the model of the new reign's honesty, and ask whether the rejection belongs to the same morality.
Conclude by weighing the Epilogue, which promises more Falstaff, against the Fleet, which is where the play actually sends him.

essayQuestions.question: How does Part 2 use the memory of Part 1?
essayQuestions.focus: Repetition, sequels and the darkening of a pattern
plan: List the shapes the play repeats: a tavern scene, a recruiting scene, a father's interview, a soliloquy on sleeplessness answering one on the sun.
Read Lady Percy's memorial in 2.3 as the play's own account of Hotspur, and note that it is used to keep a man from fighting.
Show how Falstaff's lies have changed audience: no prince counts the buckram men, only Shallow listens.
Use 3.2 and 5.3, where memory is a subject in itself, to argue that the play is about looking back.
Decide whether the sequel comments on the first play or simply completes it.

essayQuestions.question: What is the play's attitude to Prince John's conduct at Gaultree?
essayQuestions.focus: Promise, law and the absence of comment
plan: Set out exactly what is promised in 4.2 and exactly what is done, with the words 'redress' and 'grievances' in view.
Compare the Archbishop's own contempt for the multitude in 1.3, which makes him an awkward victim.
Bring in Falstaff's judgement on the sober boy in 4.3 as the only verdict the play offers.
Consider the chronicle source and the play's compression, which removes any historical excuse.
Conclude on whether silence is approval, and what the episode does to the new reign that follows it.

essayQuestions.question: Discuss the presentation of illness and age in the play.
essayQuestions.focus: The body, the state and the passage of time
plan: Start with the play's first prose line, Falstaff's water, and the Chief Justice's inventory of an old man in 1.2.
Read the Archbishop's diagnosis in 4.1 and the king's in 3.1 as the same metaphor applied to the state.
Use the Gloucestershire scenes to show time measured in dead acquaintances and market prices.
Examine the crown as bedfellow and golden care in 4.5, where the object itself is what keeps a body awake.
Close on the rejection, where white hairs are the charge against Falstaff, and ask whether the play punishes age or merely records it.

discussionQuestions: Rumour speaks first and is never seen again. Why give the play to a personification for forty lines and then drop it?
Prince John keeps his promise to the letter and hangs the men he made it to. Does the play expect us to admire him?
Hal says he cannot mourn his father in front of Poins because it would look like hypocrisy. Is that a fair description of his position?
Shallow remembers a youth Falstaff says he never had. What does the play gain from giving the memory to a liar and the correction to a bigger one?
The new king adopts one old man and rejects another in the space of three scenes. What makes the Chief Justice keepable and Falstaff not?

related.why: The first half: Shrewsbury, Hotspur and the play extempore whose 'I do, I will' is carried out here.
The reign this play ends by beginning, and the foreign quarrel Henry IV prescribed from his deathbed.
The deposition Henry IV confesses to in 4.5, and the prophecy of Northumberland's treachery that Warwick recalls in 3.1.
Both parts in one Astor volume, for reading the whole arc from Gadshill to the rejection.
Falstaff, Shallow, Pistol and the Hostess again, in a comedy where the knight's schemes fail more cheaply.
